items.body: @ayushr2 could you have a look at this one?

IIUC, we are using `go_generics` package to generate code which is using Go's native generics support. Two levels of generated code. So why not directly replace the `go_generics` atomic pointer with `atomic.Pointer`? Maybe I am missing something. Is there a benefit to doing it this way?

> 

I couldn't agree more, but stateify doesn't yet support generics. That requires the first N-1 commits in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470, so I was planning to send that after that PR (and this one) merge.
Having said that, I could move those commits to this PR, since there is some question about whether https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470 can be merged at all.

> IIUC [80913f9](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/80913f9c71a1e72d7999f736377d8bf245f873a1) requires wrapping the atomic pointer fields with a struct and putting special `stateify` tags on them. I think that is also not a very clean interface.
> 
> We should probably add native support to stateify for `atomic.Pointer`; such that it should be able to detect `atomic.Pointer` usage and generate code using .Load() and .Store(). I don't know if the AST parser we use is capable to do this.

It's not that the AST parser isn't capable, it's that that state package fundamentally wants to register a `reflect.Type` under a unique name: https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/70f9a824dc761638488b988ebd33930569a83c65/pkg/state/types.go#L339

Since there's no `reflect.Type` associated with an uninstantiated generic, we'd need to do string matching on the type's name and its methods to discover that it is an `atomic.Pointer`.

> If not, we can add support for new `stateify` tags like:
> 
> ```
> 	ptr atomic.Pointer[int] `state: pointer".(int)"`
> ```

We perhaps could, but is that any better? This would make a poor addition to `go_stateify` because it doesn't generalize beyond `atomic.Pointer`.

> 
> If you intend to cleanup `atomicptr` from go_generics, then we could also just use:
> 
> ```
> // +stateify savable
> type S struct {
> 	// descriptorTable holds descriptors.
> 	ptr atomic.Pointer[int] `state:".(int)"`
> }
> 
> func (s *S) savePtr() int {
> 	return s.ptr.Load()
> }
> 
> func (s *S) loadPtr(_ goContext.Context, ptr int) {
> 	s.ptr.Store(ptr)
> }
> ```

We could, but that feels quite manual, and ergonomically worse than what exists today.

Before the codegen deficiencies were pointed out in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470#pullrequestreview-3645103398 my goal was to remove type parameter support from go_generics, leaving only constants.

Now answering your first point:

> IIUC [80913f9](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/80913f9c71a1e72d7999f736377d8bf245f873a1) requires wrapping the atomic pointer fields with a struct and putting special `stateify` tags on them. I think that is also not a very clean interface.

Well, I don't disagree, but haven't come up with a cleaner way of supporting generics with stateify. I'm all ears for suggestions!

Restored the operation-level contract: offMu serializes operations that change the offset, including the I/O performed at that offset. The current Read, Write, and Seek implementations use plain offset accesses under offMu, so I did not restore the old claim that these accesses are atomic.

heh, this is just a function called Init, not actual init

why make assumptions?

I checked the construction path: Kernel.Init already requires an unused
kernel [1], and the test callers I inspected initialize fresh VFS objects.
So the current callers do not need these locks for exclusion; the method
name alone would not establish that.

The locks let checklocks verify the newly annotated field accesses. Its
fresh-allocation exemption does not extend to a receiver parameter [2].
We could exempt individual initialization assignments, but I prefer
keeping the short lock regions so those accesses remain checked. This
does not make concurrent calls to Init supported.

[2]: https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/309599c1e/tools/checklocks/analysis.go#L751-L771

requires exclusive access, but checklocks cannot infer that from a
receiver parameter. The locks keep those field writes checked.

Minor nit on this comment: `valueIndices` is local to `NewField` and does not escape `NewField`. What ensures `v` escapes to the heap is that `allowedValues` (and `valuesSorted`) are stored into the returned `Field` struct, which callers assign to package-level vars or long-lived metric objects. For small fields ($\le 48$), `valuesSorted` is not constructed and `valueIndices` is dropped, but `v` is still retained in `Field.values`.

Changed construction to retain the pointers in the preallocated sorted slice and updated the comment in 13e28b4f1. One subtlety: a map can remain local while pointer values stored in it escape; Go 1.26.3's [map0 test](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.3/test/escape_map.go#L13-L22) demonstrates this. Indexed slice stores likewise make the pointees escape ([slice6](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.3/test/escape_slice.go#L62-L68)), preserving stable heap addresses here. Small fields only use pointer equality.

prs.head: e0f75c3ea08d7b74e1c757e9034285142c551309

items.body:
Rebased onto current master, @EtiennePerot.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

> Is this really necessary? How tightly constrained are such workers?

In response to [your review](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15061#pullrequestreview-5399663055):

The original run was OOM-killed while enumerating tests, before any syscall case ran. It used a 300 MB scheduling estimate; I don't have evidence of the worker's hard memory limit. There are five parameterized tests, and [GoogleTest retains a parameter copy for each](https://github.com/google/googletest/blob/52eb8108c/googletest/include/gtest/internal/gtest-param-util.h#L402-L410). With two 32 MiB strings per parameter, that is at least 320 MiB of payload for registration alone, plus temporary copies.

After this change, all 50 cases passed in native and each of the two systrap variants with the same worker estimate. The actual 32 MiB syscall buffers are unchanged. The noncopying comparison also avoids duplicating and concatenating those large buffers while a case runs.

[Original run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/980d63fa-55b9-49d3-81d5-46ff7ca7cedb) · [After-fix run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/a20482e5-86cd-4bce-aa3c-1906c0a66d4a)

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
Is this really necessary? How tightly constrained are such workers?

prs.head: 1160d751fdddfbca4b41f80db3fe28299316996f

items.body:
Rebased onto current master, @EtiennePerot.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
/gemini review

## Code Review

This pull request replaces the implicit external source downloads of the TLDK/DPDK plugin stack with pinned Bazel inputs built via `rules_foreign_cc`. It introduces several patches to support musl libc compatibility, replaces glibc's backtrace with `libbacktrace`, and adds a test for stack unwinding. The review feedback highlights three key issues: a thread-safety race condition in `capture_stack` due to concurrent redirection of the global DPDK log stream, a potential out-of-bounds write in the backtrace patch's `trace_frame` callback, and a build compatibility issue in `toolchain.bzl` where standard environments might fail the strict compiler check.

This adapter is compiled only into `backtrace_test`. Its only caller is
`TestDumpStack`, which calls it twice serially; neither call starts DPDK
workers or runs in parallel. Production stack dumping does not use this
capture adapter. A mutex here would therefore add no protection needed by
the current callers, and would not serialize unrelated DPDK log writers.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

The bound follows from the pinned library's callback contract:
[`backtrace_simple` stops when the callback returns nonzero](https://github.com/ianlancetaylor/libbacktrace/blob/793921876/backtrace.h#L125-L131),
and its [implementation stops unwinding immediately](https://github.com/ianlancetaylor/libbacktrace/blob/793921876/simple.c#L83-L86).
Each dump starts with size zero. The callback writes indices 0 through
255, then returns 1, so it cannot enter again with size 256. I'll keep the
existing bound without a redundant precheck.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The strict check `toolchain.compiler not in ["gcc", "clang"]` can fail on standard environments (such as Linux with Bazel's autoconfigured toolchain) where `toolchain.compiler` is set to `"compiler"`. Since DPDK's makefiles and `rules_foreign_cc` already handle compiler compatibility and detection, this strict check is unnecessary and can be safely removed to avoid breaking the build on standard setups.

```suggestion
    toolchain = find_cc_toolchain(ctx)
```

The pinned rules_cc detector [returns `gcc` or `clang` for those compilers;
`compiler` is its fallback](https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_cc/blob/21e14308c/cc/private/toolchain/unix_cc_configure.bzl#L290-L295).
Here the compiler identifier also selects DPDK's configuration through
`RTE_TARGET = x86_64-native-linuxapp-$(C_COMPILER)`. Removing this check
would pass the unsupported `compiler` configuration to DPDK rather than
make that toolchain work. I'll retain the explicit GCC/Clang requirement.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

I compared the existing pointer, map, and slice state benchmarks on both
sides of this change. None of the six encoding/decoding cases showed a
statistically significant timing difference in this run; their median
allocation counts and bytes per operation were unchanged.

I also benchmarked `tcpip.ReceivableControlMessages` with a nonzero
`Timestamp`, so this measures the old UnixNano hook against the new binary
codec through a real caller:

| Operation | Before | After | Change | Allocs before → after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Save | 9.710 µs | 12.207 µs | +25.72% | 80 → 94 |
| Load | 12.674 µs | 13.997 µs | +10.44% | 138 → 151 |

Allocated bytes increased from 5,624 to 6,528 per save and from 6,024 to
6,320 per load. The encoded message grew from 494 to 521 bytes. The time
comparison was significant for save (p<0.001) and load (p=0.015), with ten
samples per version.

Both binaries were compiled first, then measured in ten alternating
before/after pairs on one Linux AMD EPYC worker, pinned to the same CPU
with GOMAXPROCS=1 and Go 1.27.1. Each benchmark used a 500 ms duration;
two warmups were excluded. These are state-serialization microbenchmarks,
not whole-sandbox checkpoint timings, and the timestamp comparison does
not isolate reflection from the changed representation.

The [run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/003fd04d-7d4e-4f55-9a77-584d353c93ab)
retains all raw samples and benchstat output. All 22 benchmark actions and
benchstat passed. The parent failed afterward because cleanup named two
source files deleted by the candidate; the source tree was already clean.
The measurements were preserved and not rerun.

Updated in [bfeafd451](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/bfeafd451).
Type names, fields and codec dispatch are now cached at registration;
Save/Load no longer constructs an adapter for each binary-coded value.

The follow-up `benchstat` comparison uses the same timestamp-bearing
`tcpip.ReceivableControlMessages` value for all three implementations:

```text
Measure               Original hooks   Initial codec   Revised
Save (us/call)                  8.066           9.351     6.881
Load (us/call)                 10.164          10.991     8.813
Save (allocs/call)                 80              94        68
Load (allocs/call)                138             151       125
Encoded bytes                    494             521       521
```

Relative to the original conversion hooks, Save is 14.70% faster and
Load is 13.29% faster (both p<0.001, n=12). Compared with the initial
codec implementation, they are 26.41% and 19.81% faster. The 27-byte
encoding increase remains.

The ordinary map-decoding control measured 324.9 ns/op versus 331.5 for
the original implementation (no significant difference, p=.682). It was
2.49% slower than the initial codec implementation (317.0 ns/op,
p=.008). An [earlier comparison](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/d67982e1-db7e-40c6-a307-52e95aa38215)
measured a 5.88% slowdown against that implementation; its cause remains
unestablished.

The [run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/91d7662c-227f-4afd-bdc2-e465c4f117e2)
used one Linux AMD64 worker, precompiled binaries, fixed CPU affinity,
and twelve balanced three-version blocks. The measured sources were
[original hooks](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/6500a6c00),
[initial codec](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/b27217132), and
[revised codec](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/a8081ccb5); the
amendment preserves that implementation after rebasing. These are
focused
serialization measurements, not complete-checkpoint or application
throughput results.

Updated the codec dispatch to use type switches while preserving
Register(Type). Explicit state methods take precedence, Type-only empty
structs retain their existing behavior, and binary codecs handle the
remaining registered foreign structs. Names and fields still come from
the existing type databases.

The comparison used the original hooks, the previous cached-flag codec,
and this switch on one worker, with 12 balanced blocks of the same
pointer/map/slice and ReceivableControlMessages benchmarks. Compilation
completed before measurement, with no fresh compilation during samples.
All versions use the same benchmark bodies; original to switch includes
the full codec change.

```text
                         Original    Cached flag    Type switch
Timestamp save (us/op)      9.5225       8.4035         8.2445
Timestamp load (us/op)     12.2540      10.6320        10.5390
Save allocations/op           80           68             68
Load allocations/op          138          125            125
Encoded bytes                 494          521            521
```

The switch showed no statistically significant timing difference from
the cached-flag version across all eight benchmarks. Timestamp save and
load each used 96 fewer bytes per operation, with unchanged allocation
counts. Compared with the original hooks, timestamp save was 13.42%
faster and load was 14.00% faster in this sample (p < .001); none of the
six ordinary benchmarks showed a significant timing difference.

These are focused state-codec measurements, not whole-checkpoint results
or proof of equivalent performance. The larger binary time format also
preserves zero values and numeric zone offsets. This version and these
measurements do not include BinaryAppender.

This pull request updates the TCP CUBIC congestion control implementation to comply with RFC 9438. Key changes include tracking the window at the start of an epoch with cwndEpoch, updating the Reno-friendly window estimate calculation based on received ACKs, and introducing HandleWindowRestart to manage idle periods. return c.C*t*t*t + max(c.WMax, c.cwndEpoch)

## Code Review

This pull request initializes the EndSequence field in the rackControl struct and introduces a new test, TestRACKInitialDeliverySequence, to ensure correct behavior with initial sequence numbers. The reviewer identified an additional issue where RTTSeq should also be initialized to the initial sequence number (iss) to prevent incorrect sequence comparisons when the ISN is in the upper half of the sequence space, and provided a code suggestion to address this.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Similar to `EndSequence` and `FACK`, `RTTSeq` is a sequence number field (`seqnum.Value`) in `rackControl` used for sequence comparisons (specifically in `updateRACKReorderWindow` to filter DSACKs once per round trip). If `RTTSeq` is left uninitialized (defaulting to `0`), and the connection's ISN is in the upper half of the sequence number space (i.e., `iss > 2^31`), the comparison `snd.SndUna.LessThan(rc.RTTSeq)` (which evaluates `(iss + 1).LessThan(0)`) will incorrectly evaluate to `true` on the very first ACK. This causes any DSACK received on the first ACK to be prematurely ignored. Initializing `rc.RTTSeq` to `iss` prevents this sequence comparison bug.

```suggestion
rc.EndSequence = iss
	rc.RTTSeq = iss
```

Thanks, confirmed. RTTSeq now starts at the connection ISN too. The
regression covers the first DSACK expansion, suppression within the same
round, and expansion after the round boundary for low, high and wrapping
ISNs. The original high/wrap cases fail; the corrected TCP/RACK suites on
both CPUs, focused race coverage and owning analyzers pass.

prs.title: Update PHP runtime tests to 8.5.11
prs.head: 86d8fdafd1c655385cec92f65f19a0aadfe15645

items.body: We should try unexcluding tests and seeing if they now pass with latest gVisor. Everytime I've updated the runtime version for these tests, i've had to bring this file up to date

What do you think about changing the semantics so that these entries are expected failures rather than skips? 

That warrants broader discussion because it will cause ordinary feature work to occasionally flip a test from failing to passing.

It's not clear to me why runtime updates are the obvious right time to update these fixtures though (other than to add new tests that are failing)

Retried all five excluded cases on the current gVisor qualification
branch in both directfs and goferfs modes. PHP reports each as
`SKIP: I/O capture test`; none failed or executed its test body.

PHP now [detects non-terminal standard streams itself](https://github.com/php/php-src/commit/831597748),
so I removed the redundant CSV exclusions and their BUILD reference.
The skip decision now belongs to PHP, and these cases can run when a
terminal is available.

[Validation run](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/actions/runs/39091482142).
